items.prompt: Which term describes a clear picture of the future state a leader wants the team or organisation to reach?

options.label: Quota
Vision
Audit
Budget

rubric: A vision is the picture of a desired future that sets direction.
Budget, audit and quota are management tools, not direction-setting statements.

items.prompt: What does 'accountability' mean in a team?

options.label: Holding the most senior job title and so having the final say on decisions
Being answerable for your commitments and their results
Avoiding open disagreement with teammates so that the group stays harmonious
Receiving a reward or public recognition for every task you finish

rubric: Accountability means owning commitments and outcomes.
Distractors confuse it with status, rewards or harmony.

items.prompt: Which leadership style is defined by the leader making decisions alone and telling the team what to do?

options.label: Autocratic
Laissez-faire
Coaching
Democratic

rubric: Autocratic leaders decide alone and direct others.
Democratic involves the group; laissez-faire leaves decisions to the team; coaching develops people.

items.prompt: Which of these is a SMART goal characteristic?

options.label: Measurable
Maximal
Mandatory
Managed

rubric: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
The other words sound plausible but are not part of the acronym.

items.prompt: What is 'delegation' in leadership?

options.label: Assigning a task and the authority to do it to someone else
Reviewing each step of a task before the work is allowed to continue
Doing the most important tasks yourself to ensure quality
Asking the team to vote on every decision made

rubric: Delegation hands over a task along with the needed authority.
Distractors describe doing it yourself, voting or micromanaging.

items.prompt: Which of the following are commonly recognised elements of building trust in a team? Select all that apply.

options.label: Taking credit for others' work
Withholding information to stay in control
Being open and honest
Keeping promises

rubric: Reliability and honesty build trust.
Withholding information and credit-taking erode it.

items.prompt: A new team leader wants to give her team a reason for their work that goes beyond daily tasks. She prepares a short statement describing why the team exists and what it hopes to achieve. What is this statement most commonly called?

options.label: A performance review
A risk register
A job description
A mission statement

rubric: A mission statement states purpose and aims.
Other documents cover roles, evaluation or risks.

items.prompt: Why does a leader explain the reason behind a goal rather than only stating the task?

options.label: People are more motivated when they understand the purpose
It removes the need for later follow-up once people agree
It shows the leader holds more authority than the team
It makes people follow the instructions more exactly as given

rubric: Understanding purpose raises motivation and commitment.
Distractors misread explanation as formality, a replacement for follow-up or a show of power.

items.prompt: Which example best shows 'leading by example'?

options.label: A leader who posts a clear rule about punctuality on the wall
A leader who publicly reprimands anyone who arrives late
A leader who emails the team a weekly reminder about punctuality
A leader who is always on time and expects the same of others

rubric: Leading by example means modelling the behaviour you expect.
Other options communicate or enforce but do not model.

items.prompt: How does influence differ from authority?

options.label: Influence depends on holding a job title; authority grows from personal friendship
Influence relies on force or threats; authority relies on persuading people
Influence persuades people to act; authority comes from a formal position
Influence lasts only a short while; authority stays fixed once it is given

rubric: Influence is persuasion without needing position; authority is formal power.
Distractors reverse or distort the two ideas.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why a leader gives specific, timely feedback?

options.label: It builds a documented record of faults the leader can use at the year-end review
It replaces the need to set clear goals, because people learn expectations from corrections
It ensures the team avoids repeating any mistake, so later coaching is unnecessary
It shows people what to continue or change while it is still relevant

rubric: Specific, timely feedback guides current behaviour.
Distractors treat feedback as record-keeping, perfection or a substitute for goals.

items.prompt: Which situation is the best example of a democratic leadership style?

options.label: The leader leaves the team to work alone and rarely steps in
The leader asks the team for input, then the group agrees on a plan
The leader picks the plan alone, then explains it to the team afterwards
The leader copies the plan used by another team that worked well

rubric: Democratic leadership involves the team in decisions.
Other options show autocratic, laissez-faire or borrowed approaches.

items.prompt: Which of the following explain why psychological safety helps a team perform? Select all that apply.

options.label: People feel able to raise problems early
People are more willing to admit mistakes and learn
People wait for the leader to approve every idea
People avoid speaking so conflict never arises

rubric: Safety encourages speaking up and learning.
Silence and dependence are signs of low safety.

items.prompt: A team member is new and unsure how to do a task. The leader walks through the steps, checks progress often and answers questions. Which leadership approach is this best described as?

options.label: Autocratic, making every decision alone and ignoring the person's questions
Laissez-faire, leaving the person alone to learn by trial and error
Delegating, handing off full ownership of the task to the person at once
Directing, giving clear guidance to someone who needs it

rubric: A new learner needs directing with explicit steps.
Delegating and laissez-faire give too little support; autocratic ignores input, which the leader did not do.

items.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes leading from managing?

options.label: Leading sets direction and wins commitment; managing organises work and resources to deliver plans
Leading is only for senior roles, while managing is what anyone does when supervising a task
Leading means giving orders and checking results; managing means asking opinions and building consensus
Leading handles budgets and schedules; managing sets direction and builds a shared sense of purpose

rubric: Leadership is about direction and commitment, while management is about organising work to deliver plans.
Distractor 1 swaps the two roles, and distractor 2 wrongly ties leadership to seniority.

items.prompt: Why does a clear shared vision help to motivate a team?

options.label: It makes rewards and recognition unnecessary because people work only for the mission
It removes the need for individual goals because everyone follows the same plan automatically
It guarantees agreement so that debate and disagreement no longer occur within the team
It lets people see how their daily work contributes to something that matters to them

rubric: A shared vision gives everyday tasks meaning by linking them to a common purpose.
Distractors treat vision as a replacement for goals, rewards or healthy debate, which it is not.

items.prompt: Which description best captures psychological safety in a team?

options.label: Members are shielded from critical feedback because the leader filters what they hear
Members feel able to raise concerns and admit mistakes without fear of being humiliated
Members have guaranteed job security whatever their performance results turn out to be
Members avoid conflict so that discussions stay pleasant and decisions are made quickly

rubric: Psychological safety means people can speak up and admit errors without fear of punishment or embarrassment.
Distractors confuse it with job security, conflict avoidance or protection from feedback.

items.prompt: What does accountability mean in a healthy team?

options.label: Owning commitments and outcomes, and explaining and learning from results that fall short
Tracking every task so closely that nobody can miss a commitment without being noticed
The leader taking responsibility for every result so that members never feel any pressure
Finding who caused a failure so that the person can be penalised in front of colleagues

rubric: Accountability is owning commitments and outcomes and learning from shortfalls.
Distractors confuse it with blame, with leader-only responsibility, or with close surveillance.

items.prompt: A team member with no formal authority persuades colleagues to adopt her method because it has repeatedly worked well. Which kind of influence is this?

options.label: Expertise-based influence, which is earned by showing results that others can see
Positional influence, which comes from holding a senior job title in the organisation
Coercive influence, which relies on the threat of penalties for those who do not comply
Reward-based influence, which relies on offering bonuses to those who go along with it

rubric: She has credibility earned through demonstrated results, so this is expertise-based influence.
Other options require a title, penalties or rewards, none of which she has.

items.prompt: Which behaviours help a leader build trust with a team? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keeping information limited so that the team is not distracted
Praising only the top performers in public to set the standard
Sharing the reasons behind decisions, not just the decisions
Admitting their own mistakes openly in front of the team
Keeping promises, or explaining early when one cannot be kept

rubric: Reliability, honesty about mistakes and transparency about reasons all build trust.
Withholding information and selective praise erode trust and fairness.

items.prompt: A leader must move a project deadline a week earlier. She tells the team about the client's contract change, shows what work will be cut to make room, and invites questions. The team grumbles but cooperates. Which principle best explains their cooperation?

options.label: Compensation: people comply because the leader hints that extra pay will follow later
Transparency about reasons: people accept hard news when they understand why it is needed
Fear of consequences: people comply because they expect penalties if they refuse
Clear authority: people comply because the leader holds the senior title in the team

rubric: Explaining the reasons openly builds trust and makes people willing to accept difficult changes.
Other options rest on title, fear or pay, none of which the leader used.

items.prompt: Priya is experienced, confident and has written this kind of report many times. You need another one. Which approach best fits?

options.label: Ask her to wait for your approval before each section is written to keep a consistent style
Hand over the whole report with the desired outcome and deadline, and stay available for questions
Give her step-by-step instructions and check each stage, because the report is important
Write the report yourself to guarantee quality, so she can spend time on other work

rubric: For a capable, confident person, delegating the outcome with autonomy fits and motivates.
Directing or doing it yourself suits novices and wastes her skill.

items.prompt: You lead a customer support team and want a goal for the quarter. Which goal is best written?

options.label: Be recognised as the best support team in the whole company by the end of the year
Cut average first-response time from 8 hours to 4 hours by the end of the quarter
Improve our response times a great deal as soon as we possibly can this quarter
Work harder on tickets and communicate with customers in a better way from now on

rubric: A good goal is specific, measurable and time-bound, as the response-time target is.
The others are vague, unmeasurable or lack a clear target.

items.prompt: A team member keeps interrupting colleagues in meetings. Which feedback statement best applies good feedback practice?

options.label: Some people have said meetings feel a bit uncomfortable lately, so maybe give that some thought
Great energy today, keep it up, and maybe let others speak sometimes if you happen to remember
In today's meeting you interrupted Sam twice and he stopped sharing ideas; please let people finish
You are a poor listener and always dominate meetings, which is why people dislike working with you

rubric: Effective feedback names a specific observed behaviour, its impact and a clear request.
Others label the person, stay vague or bury the message in praise.

items.prompt: Your team missed a deadline because a handoff between two members was unclear. Which response best applies accountability?

options.label: Send a reminder of the deadline policy to everyone and then move on to the next task
Hold a blame-free review of what happened, then agree owners and dates for the fixes
Quietly reassign the work and say nothing, so morale is not lowered any further
Ask who dropped the handoff and note it in that person's performance review

rubric: A blame-free review with named owners and dates builds accountability and fixes the cause.
Punishing, ignoring or issuing generic reminders does not address the unclear handoff.

items.prompt: Two team members each insist their task should be done first and both ask you to decide. Which action best applies leadership practice?

options.label: Let the louder person win so the argument ends quickly and work can keep moving forward
Bring both back to the shared goal and agree priority by which task serves it best
Pick the more senior person's task to show respect for their experience and tenure
Tell both to work it out alone, since that builds independence and conflict skills

rubric: Anchoring the decision in the shared goal gives a fair, transparent basis for priority.
Other options reward volume or seniority, or avoid the leader's role.

items.prompt: You are launching a new team goal. Which actions fit good leadership practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Check in regularly on progress and help remove obstacles
Set the milestones yourself so the plan stays consistent and no one has to debate it
Explain why the goal matters to customers and to the team
Focus the launch message on the targets and deadlines, and leave out the reasons to avoid distracting people

items.prompt: You lead a new team of five people from different departments. After a week, members are unsure who does what, and several are waiting for others to start. What is the best first step?

options.label: Organise a social event first so relationships form, and leave roles for later discussion
Assign tasks privately by email without explaining the overall goal to anyone
Run a kickoff to agree the goal, clarify each role and decide who makes which decisions
Wait a few weeks so natural roles emerge without any imposed structure from you

rubric: New teams need a shared goal and clear roles first; a kickoff provides both.
Waiting, private assignments without context, or delaying roles keep the confusion going.

items.prompt: A new analyst is eager but has never produced a variance report. Using situational leadership, which style fits best at this point?

options.label: Delegating: hand over the report and review only the final result
Directing: give step-by-step instructions and check progress often
Observing: let them try alone first and discuss mistakes afterward
Supporting: ask for their ideas and leave the method to them

rubric: A learner with high enthusiasm but low skill needs clear direction and frequent checks.
Delegating and supporting suit people who already have the skill; observing leaves a novice without guidance.

items.prompt: A leader wants to turn the vague aim 'improve customer service' into a SMART goal for a support team. Which version is best?

options.label: Raise first-response satisfaction from 78% to 85% by 30 June using weekly case reviews
Raise customer satisfaction scores across all channels by 20 points within one month by running daily coaching
Deliver excellent service on every call by always following the company values and the service charter
Reduce all customer complaints to zero across every region by next month through stricter call monitoring

rubric: The key is specific, measurable, time-bound and realistic, with a named method.
Distractors are vague, unrealistic or unmeasurable.

items.prompt: A leader wants to give feedback using the Situation-Behavior-Impact model. Which statement follows it?

options.label: In Tuesday's client call you interrupted Sam twice, and he stopped sharing his analysis.
You are generally disrespectful in meetings, and people notice that attitude.
In Tuesday's client call you seemed rude, which shows you don't value colleagues.
Please try to be more collaborative in future client calls with the whole team.

rubric: SBI names a specific situation, an observable behaviour and its concrete impact.
Distractors judge character or give vague advice instead of describing observable behaviour.

items.prompt: A leader wants to develop a capable team member who is ready to grow, while keeping accountability for results. Which task is best to delegate?

options.label: Handle a confidential disciplinary meeting about one of their peers
Redo a task the leader enjoys, following every step as prescribed
Lead a vendor negotiation within agreed limits, with a mid-point check-in
Fix a crisis due in two hours on a system they have never seen

rubric: Good developmental delegation is a meaningful task with clear boundaries and a checkpoint.
Distractors are inappropriate, too risky or too controlled to build growth.

items.prompt: A reliable team member misses a deadline for the first time, delaying two colleagues. What should the leader do first?

options.label: Raise it at the next team meeting so the standard is clear to everyone
Reassign the work quietly and say nothing so morale stays intact
Meet privately, ask what happened, and agree a concrete recovery plan
Issue a written warning now so a precedent exists for later deadlines

rubric: A private conversation to understand the cause and reset the agreement fits a first lapse by a reliable person.
Public shaming, silence and premature formal action each damage trust or skip accountability.

items.prompt: You are announcing a new strategic direction to your team. Which actions apply good practice for building shared direction? Select all that apply.

options.label: Send one detailed email and treat silence as agreement
Quote only board-level financial targets so the message stays objective
Ask members to restate the goal in their own words to check understanding
Repeat the message across several settings over the following weeks
Explain why the change matters and link it to each person's daily work

rubric: Shared direction needs meaning, checked understanding and repetition.
Silence is not agreement, and financial targets alone rarely connect to people's work.

items.prompt: Priya is a highly skilled engineer who has become withdrawn and slower since a failed launch. She still knows the work well, and her leader suspects a loss of confidence. Using situational leadership, which approach should the leader take?

options.label: Supporting: listen, encourage her, and share decisions while she picks the method
Directing: prescribe each task and check her output daily until speed returns
Delegating: leave her entirely alone so she can recover without pressure
Reassigning: move her to simpler work until her confidence comes back

rubric: Skilled but low-confidence people need high support and low direction.
Directing undermines a capable person; delegating alone gives no support; reassigning wastes skill.

items.prompt: Team members stay silent in meetings but raise concerns privately afterwards. Last month the leader publicly corrected one member's error. What is the most likely cause of the silence?

options.label: The team is naturally introverted and prefers to think alone, so written updates would suit it better than live discussion
Meetings run too long and have crowded agendas, so attention drops and people disengage from the discussion
Members lack the technical depth to contribute confidently in the room, so targeted coaching is needed first
Being corrected in front of peers signalled that speaking up risks embarrassment, lowering psychological safety

rubric: Private concerns after a public correction point to reduced psychological safety.
Distractors blame knowledge, length or personality without explaining why concerns appear privately.

items.prompt: A leader pays bonuses for ticket counts. Staff hit targets, but show no interest in product quality or improvement ideas. What does this analysis show?

options.label: Rewards secure the measured output but don't build commitment to a shared purpose
Bonuses were too small to motivate, so larger ones would fix quality
Staff lack the capability for quality work, so tighter supervision is needed
Targets were unclear, so more detailed metrics will align effort again

rubric: A purely transactional approach gets the rewarded behaviour but not commitment to purpose.
Distractors assume more reward, supervision or metrics will fix a motivation-quality gap.

items.prompt: A top salesperson is promoted to manager. Team results fall while she personally closes more deals than ever. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: She still defines success as her own output, so she isn't developing others
Her team is too junior, so replacing them would restore results
She lacks sales knowledge for the territory, so product training is needed
She is too friendly with the team, so stricter targets would restore results

rubric: Rising personal output with falling team results shows she hasn't shifted from doing to leading.
Other options misattribute the cause to knowledge, team quality or tone.

items.prompt: A leader's proposal stalls with a peer department head despite strong data. Which diagnosis best explains the stall?

options.label: The peer resists all change, so waiting for new leadership is the only option
The data needs more detail, so additional charts will overcome the objection
The peer lacks authority, so escalating to their boss will force agreement
The proposal ignores what the peer gains or loses, so they have no reason to back it

rubric: Influence without authority depends on addressing the other party's interests.
Distractors lean on more data, force or waiting instead of understanding interests.

items.prompt: A team that volunteered to mentor interns stops after the company starts paying cash per intern mentored. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: The payment was so high that it created resentment among non-mentors, who then pressured the mentors to quit
The interns were not grateful enough, which reduced the social reward the mentors had been getting
The mentors were already overloaded, so any new incentive would have failed to keep them mentoring
Payment reframed a purpose-driven act as a transaction, reducing intrinsic motivation

rubric: Extrinsic rewards can crowd out intrinsic motivation for tasks people value.
Other options introduce factors not suggested by the situation.

items.prompt: Which observations point to a trust deficit in a team rather than a skill gap? Select all that apply.

options.label: New hires need longer than expected to learn the process
Members copy the leader on every email to protect themselves
Members give vague answers in retrospectives after earlier candid comments were used against them
Quality drops on a new tool nobody has been trained to use
Errors surface only after customers report them, never from team members

rubric: Hidden errors, self-protective behaviour and guarded feedback signal low trust.
Tool-training and onboarding delays are skill or learning issues.

items.prompt: A leader delegates a project to Marcus, then asks for daily updates and rewrites his drafts. Marcus now waits for approval before every step, and the leader complains he lacks initiative. What best explains the situation?

options.label: The project was too large for one person, so splitting it into smaller parts would restore his initiative
Marcus lacks the skill for this work, so delegation should be withdrawn and each task prescribed
Constant control removed Marcus's ownership, so his passivity is a response to the leader's behaviour
Daily updates were too infrequent for him, so hourly check-ins would give him the clarity he needs

rubric: Delegation with constant control removes ownership, and the passivity is a result of that behaviour.
Distractors blame ability, size or too little oversight, which would worsen the problem.

items.prompt: A team meets every deadline, yet members rarely flag problems early and surprises surface at launch. The leader publicly thanks whoever 'saves' late projects. Which analysis best explains the pattern?

options.label: The team is too cohesive, so groupthink stops anyone seeing risks that outsiders would normally notice early
Rewarding last-minute rescues signals that hidden problems are valued over early warnings, so people wait to escalate
Members are not committed to deadlines, so firmer penalties for any reported slip would raise early honesty
The team lacks the technical skill to spot problems, so issues only become visible once testing starts near launch

rubric: Public praise for rescues teaches people that late heroics earn recognition, so early escalation is discouraged.
Distractors blame skill, commitment or cohesion instead of the incentive the leader's own behaviour creates.

items.prompt: After a reorganisation, a highly skilled analyst who used to be energetic now does minimal work and avoids meetings. Her manager responds with detailed step-by-step task instructions. What is the main flaw in that response?

options.label: It ignores that high performers should be left alone entirely, because contact during change reduces their autonomy
It treats a motivation and confidence problem as a skill gap, so directing adds friction instead of restoring commitment
It focuses on one individual, when reorganisations affect everyone equally and need a team-wide written update
It gives too little structure, since skilled people in transition need more precise task definitions than before

rubric: The analyst is capable but has lost commitment, so supportive listening and clarity of purpose fit better than directing.
Distractors misread the situation as needing more structure, total hands-off, or only a broadcast message.

items.prompt: A director presents an inspiring three-year vision twice. Weeks later, team leads still ask what they should start or stop doing. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: The vision is not translated into team-level priorities and trade-offs, so it inspires but does not guide decisions
Team leads resist change by nature, so the director should replace the sceptics before repeating the message
The vision is too ambitious, so people dismiss it; a smaller target would give leads clearer daily decisions
The message was delivered too rarely, so repeating it weekly in the same words will eventually produce clarity

rubric: Leads need priorities and trade-offs that connect the vision to their daily choices.
Distractors blame ambition, people or frequency rather than the missing translation into action.

items.prompt: In weekly meetings a group agrees 'we'll update the client pricing', yet the task is done late or twice by different people. Which element is most likely missing?

options.label: A single named owner with a date, so no one can assume someone else is handling it
A longer task description, because members cannot act until every step of the work is written down
More frequent meetings, because shared tasks need daily discussion before anyone feels responsible for them
A stronger consequence for lateness, since agreement without penalty never produces follow-through in any team

rubric: Diffuse ownership ('we') causes both gaps and duplicates; a named owner and date create accountability.
Distractors reach for penalties, meetings or documentation, none of which fixes unclear ownership.

items.prompt: A product lead asks the support team to log defects in a new format. Support agrees in meetings but ignores it. Support is measured on tickets closed per hour. What best explains the behaviour?

options.label: Support does not understand the reasons behind the request, so a clearer presentation of the product vision would fix it
Support lacks authority to change its own process, so the request must be escalated to a department head first
Support dislikes the product lead personally, so building the relationship is the root remedy needed here
The new format adds time per ticket and their metric punishes it, so compliance conflicts with what they are rewarded for

rubric: Influence fails when the request conflicts with the incentives the group is measured on.
Distractors assume a communication, relationship or authority problem without evidence.

items.prompt: Which observations most strongly suggest low psychological safety on a team? Select all that apply.

options.label: Junior members stay silent in meetings until the most senior person has spoken
Members rarely admit mistakes until someone else discovers them
Meetings end early because the agenda was well prepared in advance
Members argue openly about priorities, then commit to the decision
Dissent appears in private messages but not in the group discussion

rubric: Silence before seniors, concealed mistakes and private-only dissent all show people fear speaking up in the open.
Short meetings and open debate followed by commitment are normal signs of healthy teams.

items.prompt: A new manager began micromanaging every report after a defect shipped. Output has dropped and two strong engineers are interviewing elsewhere. The manager says the defect proves people need close oversight. Which analysis of this reasoning is best?

options.label: It is sound, because one shipped defect shows that autonomy must be earned back through close oversight of every report until the team has proven it can deliver reliably
It is partly sound, but oversight should be applied equally to all reports, strong engineers included, so that nobody sees the new controls as favouritism
It overlooks that the engineers' job searches, not the process, are the real cause of the defect, so retention bonuses should be tackled before anything else
It generalises from one process failure to a trait of people, ignoring that unclear review checkpoints likely caused the defect

rubric: The defect points to a missing process step; blanket oversight punishes the whole team and drives out talent.
Distractors accept the manager's premise or reverse cause and effect.

items.prompt: A data breach is found at 5pm. Criteria: contain within hours, decisions are reversible, and the team is skilled but needs coordination. Which leadership approach is best?

options.label: Wait until morning to gather a complete picture, then pick a participative approach with a rested team
Hold a full-team consensus session so everyone buys in before any containment step is taken tonight
Delegate fully to the most senior engineer and stay unavailable so the team does not feel monitored
Direct containment now, assign roles clearly, and set a review point to adjust as facts emerge

rubric: Urgency and coordination needs favour a directive style, with a review point to adapt because decisions are reversible.
Distractors trade speed for consensus, abdicate leadership, or delay containment.

items.prompt: A top-performing salesperson regularly belittles colleagues. Criteria: protect team trust, retain performance where possible, apply fair standards. Which response is best?

options.label: Give specific behavioural feedback with clear expectations and consequences, applying the same standard as for anyone
Remove the person from the team at once without feedback, to show that standards matter more than results
Move the person onto solo accounts permanently so conflicts stop, without raising the behaviour directly
Overlook the behaviour while results stay high, since team output matters more than the occasional friction

rubric: Specific feedback with consequences protects trust and fairness while giving a chance to keep the performer.
Distractors excuse the behaviour, skip due process, or avoid the issue.

items.prompt: A leader plans to seek full consensus on a vendor choice due in two days. The team is split. Criteria: buy-in, the deadline, decision quality. Which critique is most valid?

options.label: Consensus will likely miss the deadline; consult widely, then decide and explain the reasoning
Consensus is sound, but the leader should poll the team and follow the majority to share accountability for the result
Consensus is too slow, so the leader should decide alone now, since wider input would add delay but little quality
Consensus is right for a split team, so the leader should ask for an extension to protect buy-in and decision quality

rubric: With a split team and a short deadline, consult-then-decide meets all three criteria best.
Distractors over-weight consensus, avoid accountability, or discard input entirely.

items.prompt: A manager plans to boost creativity in a design team by paying a bonus per idea submitted. Which critique best judges this plan against the goal of high-quality new ideas?

options.label: Individual bonuses tend to cause rivalry and idea hoarding, so the same per-idea payment is better split across the whole team
The plan is sound, since larger rewards usually raise motivation, and more ideas submitted means more good ideas to select from
Bonuses have little effect on knowledge work, so paying per idea will leave the number and quality of ideas about unchanged
Rewarding quantity can encourage many low-quality ideas and crowd out interest, so the measure misaligns with the goal

rubric: A quantity metric misaligns with a quality goal and can displace intrinsic motivation.
Distractors make absolute claims about rewards that experienced leaders know are not true.

items.prompt: A report is client-critical and due in three days. Options: an experienced but overloaded employee, or an eager junior who needs coaching. Criteria: client risk is high, deadline is fixed, development is secondary. Which choice is best?

options.label: Split it evenly between both without a named lead, so the workload is shared and neither person feels passed over
Do it yourself, because handing a high-risk task to either person adds risk you can avoid by owning it
Give it to the junior with weekly check-ins, because a stretch task builds skills and the deadline leaves time
Assign the experienced person, lift some of their other work, and have the junior shadow

rubric: High client risk and a fixed deadline favour the experienced person, with workload relief and shadowing serving development.
Distractors ignore risk, refuse to delegate, or blur ownership.

items.prompt: A CEO plans to announce layoffs by email with no prior conversation or manager briefing. Given the goal of keeping the trust of remaining staff, which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Managers left unbriefed cannot answer questions, which leaves rumours to fill the gap
Email announcements are legally invalid in every organisation, so the plan cannot proceed
Delaying any announcement indefinitely would always be better for morale than telling people
An impersonal channel signals disregard for the people affected and for those watching
Giving no reasons or criteria undermines perceived fairness of the decision

rubric: Channel, missing rationale and unbriefed managers each damage trust among those who remain.
The legal claim is false, and indefinite delay is not a given improvement.

items.prompt: Two leads disagree. One wants quarterly stretch goals with rewards; the other wants stable goals with coaching. The team has high turnover, low burnout-survey scores and a critical launch in six months. Criteria: sustain capacity through launch while keeping ambition. Which plan is best?

options.label: Pause all goals and reviews until after launch so people can recover, then restart goal setting with fresh targets once the launch is done
Let each team member choose whichever goal style they prefer, without any shared direction before launch
Keep a few clear launch-critical goals, protect workload, coach to build capacity, and defer stretch rewards until after launch
Adopt stretch goals with quarterly rewards for everyone, since a visible prize and urgency keep a team focused and retain top performers until launch

rubric: The plan keeps direction on what matters, protects capacity and postpones stretch incentives that would worsen burnout.
Distractors push pressure, remove direction altogether, or fragment shared goals.

items.prompt: A leader must pick a style for a newly merged team where two senior engineers openly dispute the architecture, a launch is in 6 weeks, and the team is competent but divided. Criteria: preserve the deadline, retain both engineers, and keep the team's commitment to the result. Which approach best fits?

options.label: Let the two engineers keep debating until they converge, since imposed technical decisions always erode commitment in skilled teams
Hold a time-boxed decision forum where both present trade-offs against launch criteria, then the leader decides and explains the reasoning
Pick the architecture privately after consulting only the more senior engineer, since speed matters most before a launch
Put the choice to a full-team vote and adopt the majority view, since voting guarantees fairness and removes the leader from the conflict

rubric: A time-boxed forum with an explained leader decision balances voice, speed and commitment.
Open-ended consensus risks the deadline; private or vote-based decisions damage trust or ignore the criteria.

items.prompt: A leader's team has missed targets twice. Criteria: restore accountability without eroding psychological safety. Which response is best judged against them?

options.label: Review each miss jointly to find causes, then agree named owners and checkpoints for the next cycle, with consequences for ignored commitments
Ask each member to privately report who caused the misses, so the leader can address individuals one by one without opening a group debate about the failures
Lower the targets so the team regains confidence after two misses, and defer any discussion of accountability until results have clearly improved again
Replace the weakest performer publicly to signal that missed targets carry real consequences for everyone, and then reset the targets with the remaining team

rubric: Joint causal review plus clear ownership keeps accountability and safety.
Public punishment and secret reporting damage trust; lowering targets avoids accountability.

items.prompt: A founder-leader's charismatic vision drove early growth. At 200 people, decisions bottleneck on her and middle managers are disengaged. Which critique of her current approach is most defensible?

options.label: Disengagement shows managers lack commitment, so tighter oversight and approval of their daily work will restore alignment and pace
Personal influence alone does not scale; she must build decision rights and manager capability so direction works without her
Her vision has lost its pull, so she should rewrite it with more ambitious goals and present it again to re-energise the managers
The bottleneck is a temporary growth effect, so keeping decisions centralised remains the fastest route to consistency until headcount settles

rubric: Scaling requires delegated decision rights and developed managers, not only charisma.
Other options misdiagnose a structural issue as motivation, vision wording or a temporary effect.

items.prompt: Two candidates for team lead: A delivers best individual results but hoards information; B has average results but raises team capability and shares credit. Criterion: the team's long-term output over three years. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Choose B, because average performers are always more loyal and less likely to leave than top performers
Choose A, because the best performer's technical standard will set the example the team naturally copies
Choose B, because leadership output is multiplied through others and A's hoarding limits team learning and resilience
Choose A, because information habits can be fixed with a policy while individual excellence cannot be taught

rubric: Over three years, leverage through others outweighs individual output.
Distractors assume modelling excellence or policy fixes hoarding, or rest on an unsupported loyalty claim.

items.prompt: A leader announces a reorganisation after a confidential board decision and can share only part of the reasons. Criterion: maintain trust during the constraint. Which communication approach is best?

options.label: Say nothing until every detail can be shared, so that early messages never need to be corrected later
Share a simplified, positive rationale that covers the gaps so staff are not unsettled by missing information
Delegate the announcement to managers, so the leader avoids questions that touch confidential matters
State what is decided, what cannot yet be shared and why, and when more will be known, then keep that date

rubric: Honest boundaries with a commitment to follow up preserve credibility.
Filling gaps with spin, silence or delegation invites rumour and erodes trust.

items.prompt: A leader is judging whether to adopt a participative decision style for a particular decision. Which conditions favour doing so? Select all that apply.

options.label: The leader has already fixed the decision and wants approval
A genuine crisis demands action within minutes
Acceptance by the team strongly determines implementation success
Team members hold information the leader lacks

rubric: Participation pays off when knowledge sits with the team and buy-in drives execution.
Crises favour directive action, and pre-decided choices make participation a sham.

items.prompt: A division head praises a high-performing sales manager whose team hits every target but has 40% annual turnover and whose reports describe fear of her reactions. The CEO asks whether to promote her to regional director. Criteria: sustainable results and cultural impact across a larger scope. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Promote her, because targets are the objective measure of leadership and the turnover is the cost of high standards
Promote her and assign an HR partner to manage turnover, so her sales skills are rewarded and the culture is protected
Decline the promotion, because a record of fear-driven turnover shows she lacks the character for senior leadership and coaching is unlikely to help
Defer promotion until she sustains results without the fear and turnover, since a larger scope would amplify the damage

rubric: Results through fear are unsustainable and would scale harm; conditional deferral is balanced.
Other options ignore the cost, outsource it, or overstate that behaviour cannot change.

items.prompt: Design a plan for a leader taking over a team that distrusts management after layoffs. Constraints: show results within 90 days, avoid false promises, and begin rebuilding accountability. Which plan meets all three?

options.label: Spend the first 90 days on social events and team-building to rebuild goodwill, and introduce goals and owners only once trust has clearly returned
Hold an all-hands announcing a bold new vision and promise that no further layoffs will occur, then track progress against vision milestones each month
Listen one-to-one first, commit to a few small visible fixes the team named, deliver them on time, then set shared goals with clear owners
Restructure roles and metrics in the first month to show decisive control, then collect feedback from the team once the new structure has settled

rubric: Small kept commitments plus listening rebuild trust honestly and lead toward accountability.
Others make unsafe promises, delay listening, or postpone accountability.

items.prompt: Design a mechanism so decisions in a 12-team organisation stay aligned with strategy without leadership approving each one. Constraints: fast local decisions, visible accountability, and no ambiguity about direction. Which design fits?

options.label: Set a few clear priorities and decision limits, let teams decide inside them, and review outcomes openly on a regular cadence
Issue a detailed rulebook covering every common decision type, with any exception escalated to the CEO for a ruling within a set number of days
Require all decisions above a small budget to be approved by the executive team, so that every major commitment is checked against strategy before it starts
Give each team its own goals and let them coordinate informally, relying on shared culture and goodwill to keep their separate choices aligned over time

rubric: Clear priorities, boundaries and open review give autonomy, accountability and clarity.
Other options slow decisions, leave direction ambiguous, or over-specify.

items.prompt: A leader wants to build a successor for her role within 18 months. Constraints: the candidate must gain real decision experience, the team must not be put at risk, and the leader must still be accountable. Which plan satisfies all?

options.label: Delegate progressively larger decisions with agreed guardrails, debrief each one, and keep irreversible high-stakes calls until readiness is shown
Hand the candidate the role's full decision authority for six months, stay out of the way, and review only the final results at the end
Fund external leadership courses and a written assessment, and delegate real decisions only after the candidate passes every module on the programme
Have the candidate shadow her in every meeting and decision for 17 months, then hand over full authority for the final month before she steps aside

rubric: Graduated delegation with guardrails and debriefs builds experience while limiting risk.
Others risk the team, delay experience, or substitute courses for practice.

items.prompt: Design a response for a leader whose team resists a necessary change. Constraints: the change cannot be cancelled, deadlines are fixed, and the team's expertise is needed for design details. Which approach fits?

options.label: Make the change mandatory with no discussion of any aspect, so that resistance cannot spread to other teams or workstreams
Delay the announcement until the team feels ready, then ask them whether they agree to proceed with the planned rollout
Reopen the decision to team debate, since strong resistance suggests the leader's original reasoning was probably weak or incomplete
State that the change is fixed and why, then let the team decide how to implement the design details

rubric: Fixed what must be fixed, with real voice on the how, uses expertise and respects constraints.
Other options pretend choice exists, shut out expertise, or reopen a closed decision.

items.prompt: A leader wants a feedback culture in which people raise bad news early. Constraints: no anonymous-only channels, leader credibility must be demonstrated, and results should be measurable. Which design meets all?

options.label: Publish a policy requiring staff to report problems within 24 hours, with graded sanctions for late reports and a monthly count of reports filed on time
Leader openly shares her own mistakes, thanks early bad news, acts visibly on it, and tracks time-to-escalation of issues
Reward teams with no reported incidents, so that staff are motivated to keep problems under control
Run a quarterly anonymous survey on openness, publish the aggregated scores to all staff, and have the leadership team discuss the trend

rubric: Modelling, positive response, visible action and a metric satisfy all constraints.
Sanctions and rewarding zero incidents suppress reporting; surveys are anonymous-only and slow.

items.prompt: A leader designs a team charter for a cross-functional project team where members report to different managers. Constraints: need shared goals, clear accountability, and a way to resolve conflicts. Which elements should the charter include? Select all that apply.

options.label: A ban on discussing disagreements outside formal meetings
A single shared outcome with named owners for each deliverable
A rule that members follow their home manager's priorities when conflicts arise
An agreed escalation path and decision rule for disagreements

rubric: Shared outcome with owners and an escalation rule meet the three constraints.
Home-manager priority fragments goals; a ban on discussion suppresses conflict resolution.

items.prompt: A hospital unit leader must introduce a new safety checklist that senior surgeons see as insulting. Constraints: adoption within 3 months, no loss of surgeons, and evidence that it works. Which plan best meets all three?

options.label: Have nurses enforce it at the point of care, with escalation to the unit leader when a surgeon declines, so the leader avoids confronting surgeons directly
Offer it as optional for the first three months and wait until enough surgeons adopt it on their own initiative, then report the results
Recruit respected surgeons to co-design and pilot it, share early outcome data, and have leaders use it visibly before requiring it
Mandate it immediately with weekly audits and publish compliance by surgeon, so peer pressure drives adoption within the 3 months

rubric: Co-design, pilot data and modelled use build adoption and evidence without losing surgeons.
Other options risk exits, miss the deadline, or shift conflict to junior staff.
